paras: The attempted lynching of Jim Dillard took place at a political meeting in Clarendon, Monroe County, Arkansas, on Saturday, September 1, 1888, when a crowd beat and stabbed Dillard, a Black party flag-bearer, after he shot a white man and the sheriff. Two men died in the fight, William Walls and a Black spectator, John Stayton, while Dillard survived and was kept in jail away from Clarendon as armed crowds searched for him. Papers across the country ran the story as an example of violent campaigning in Arkansas.

According to a Helena dispatch to the Memphis Appeal, politics in Monroe County had been "at a fever heat" for months, with two tickets, "the people's ticket" and "the fair divide," both bidding for the Black vote. After several fights between their followers, the candidates were advertised to debate at the courthouse in Clarendon, the county seat, that Saturday afternoon.

In the Appeal's account Dillard, the Fair-divide party's flag-bearer, "became offensive" to the other side and was struck; the New York Sun said he kept interrupting the speakers until Walls knocked him down. When Walls, a young white man, rushed at him, Dillard drew a pistol and shot him in the abdomen, and Walls, falling, shot Dillard in the shoulder and leg before dying. Men rushed in on Dillard, but his friends surrounded him with pistols, clubs and knives and kept them off.

Sheriff Robinson then tried to quiet the crowd and arrest Dillard, who shot him in the hip or thigh. The crowd, which the Appeal described as inflamed "to a crazy frenzy," cut, kicked and beat Dillard but did not kill him, and the Sun added that he was stabbed. During the shooting a stray bullet struck Stayton in the forehead as he stood at the edge of the crowd, killing him.

Dillard's friends carried him off, and the Appeal's first report said he was put on a train to the Pine Bluff jail. That night armed men came to the jail "for the purpose of lynching Dillard" and then searched a St. Louis, Arkansas & Texas train, but did not find him because his friends had concealed him. A Little Rock dispatch of September 5 said instead that a deputy sheriff had taken him to Little Rock, and that "a mob of several hundred men" searched Clarendon "with the avowed purpose of swinging him up."

On September 4 an officer took Dillard back to Clarendon but, finding feeling unabated, returned him that night to the Little Rock jail until "the excitement subsides." No one in the crowd is reported to have been arrested, and no report of an inquest or of Dillard's trial appears in the coverage.

The story reached most papers through a Helena wire dispatch, credited by the New-York Tribune to the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, which ran from Maine to Oregon between September 4 and 14. Headlines cast it as campaign bloodshed, among them "A Murderous Political Brawl" in the Tribune, "Baptized in Blood" in the St. Paul Globe and "Sanguinary Campaigning in Arkansas" in the Helena, Montana, Herald. The wire text called the crowd "the mob," did not name the Black man killed, and ended with Dillard "spirited away" and "a mob is after him."

The Memphis Appeal printed the fullest account under the headline "A Riot in Monroe" and the deck "A Negro Begins Shooting Into a Crowd," while describing Stayton as "inoffensive." Its follow-up two days later, headed "Desperado Dillard," called him "the negro desperado who killed another negro and white man" and reported the mob's aim to hang him without comment. Weekly news summaries shortened it further, some saying Dillard killed both men and one listing a Clarendon riot "on the 3d" with three men killed.

Accounts differ on the deaths: the wire and the Appeal said Dillard fired once and a stray bullet killed Stayton, while a Pine Bluff dispatch in the Rock Island Argus said Wall's shot at Polk Montgomery killed Stayton and Dillard then shot Wall twice more. The Argus also said Dillard fired at the sheriff and missed, and the Sun reported a dozen wounded, a figure no other paper gave.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Jim Dillard
bases: A crowd beat, cut and stabbed Jim Dillard after he shot William Walls and the sheriff at a political meeting, and armed crowds then hunted him at the jail, on a train and in Clarendon to lynch him, but he survived (A2, A3, A4, A12).

Crowds beat Dillard and twice sought him 'for the purpose of lynching' after he shot Walls and the sheriff, but he survived in custody (A2, A12); the two deaths came from the exchange of shots in the fight, not from the mob (A1, A2, A3).

Independent Pine Bluff, Helena and Little Rock dispatches agree on the shooting at Clarendon, the mob's beating of Dillard and the effort to lynch him, though they differ on who killed whom (A1, A2, A3, A12).

accounts.label: Helena wire report
accounts.gist: Walls tried to strike Dillard, who shot him; Walls shot Dillard twice and died; Dillard's armed friends held off the mob, he shot the sheriff, the mob beat him, a stray bullet killed a Black spectator, and Dillard was 'spirited away' with a mob after him.

accounts.label: Eye-witness via Helena (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: Dillard 'became offensive' and was struck before Walls rushed him; after the crowd cut and beat him, friends put him on a train to the Pine Bluff jail, where armed men came that night to lynch him and then searched a train.

accounts.label: Pine Bluff dispatch (Rock Island Argus)
accounts.gist: Someone threw a club at Dilliard, who shot Wall; Wall's shot at Polk Montgomery killed Stayton; Dilliard shot Wall twice more, killing him, and fired at the sheriff but missed.

accounts.label: Variant Helena report (New York Sun)
accounts.gist: A night meeting ended in a riot with two killed and a dozen wounded; Dillard insulted the speakers and Walls knocked him down before the shooting; the mob beat and stabbed Dillard.

accounts.label: Little Rock special (Memphis Appeal)
accounts.gist: A deputy took the wounded Dillard to Little Rock; several hundred men searched Clarendon to hang him, and an attempt to return him there failed because feeling had not abated.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the Helena wire under headlines that cast it as campaign bloodshed ('A Murderous Political Brawl', 'Baptized in Blood', 'An Arkansas Riot') and called the crowd 'the mob'.
The Memphis Appeal blamed 'A Negro' for 'Shooting Into a Crowd' and later called Dillard a 'negro desperado', while describing Stayton as 'inoffensive' and reporting the mob's lynching aim plainly.
